analysis.body:
# Interconnection Queue Analysis for Data Center Operations

The eight states tracked in commercial electricity sales consumed 54,798 MWh in June 2026, with Texas accounting for 15,754 MWh at an average price of $8.66 per MWh—the lowest among major data center hubs. California's 10,025 MWh cost $27.33 per MWh, making it the most expensive region despite ranking second in volume. Virginia, Georgia, and Ohio each consumed between 5,500 and 7,700 MWh, with Virginia priced at $10.99 and Georgia at $11.91, offering moderate cost profiles for large-footprint operations. These figures serve as a proxy for data center load rather than a direct measurement, since data centers occupy the commercial billing class alongside offices and retail.

Across the four major grid interconnection queues, 8,377 generator projects totaling 1.33 million MW await connection—a figure dominated by solar (328,000 MW), storage (326,000 MW), wind (169,000 MW), and gas (184,000 MW). ERCOT's Texas queue alone holds 438,086 MW in 1,778 requests, with gas and storage comprising 238,000 MW combined. MISO's 299,721 MW spread across 3,846 requests shows the highest solar concentration (146,000 MW) and the largest number of individual projects. These queues represent planned generation and storage infrastructure, which tend to track data center load growth since operators size their power supply to anticipated demand.

Storage capacity in the queues—159,820 MW in ERCOT, 67,027 MW in MISO, 52,513 MW in Southwest Power Pool, and 46,870 MW in CAISO—totals 326,230 MW and reflects the grid's adaptation to variable renewable input and round-the-clock data center demand. Gas projects similarly distribute across regions: ERCOT leads with 78,092 MW, followed by Southwest Power Pool at 47,222 MW, suggesting that Texas and south-central utilities plan substantial peaking capacity alongside renewables. Watch for which storage and gas projects move from queue to construction phase, as their completion timelines will signal whether generation can meet the sustained, high-capacity-factor demand that AI workloads impose.
